lines.text: A loop is how you tell the computer to do something over and over, without writing it out over and over.
You do this already. Think about washing up.
You haven't got a plan that says wash the first plate, then wash the second plate, then wash the third one. You've got one instruction — wash a plate — and you keep going until the sink's empty.
The instruction never changes. What changes is which plate is in your hand.
The pile is the sink. Each time round, plate is the one you're holding right now. When there's nothing left in the pile, the loop stops by itself.
You never count, and you never have to tell it when to stop.
Sometimes though, you do want to count. Do this five times. Go along a row of six squares. Then you say it like this instead.
Three things in those brackets, and they come in the order you'd say them out loud.
Start at zero. Keep going while i is under six. Add one each time round.
So i is zero, then one, two, three, four, five — and then it stops, because six isn't under six.
And yes, it starts at zero. Computers count from zero, not one. It feels wrong for about a week, and then you stop noticing.
